rationale: A wins because it has the discipline to keep the provable story: "Flat fee vs. interchange: the math behind Plaid's \"up to 70% cheaper\" claim" and to refuse "Pay by bank finally takes off in the US" as unsupported. B's "Bank-to-bank payments have flopped at checkout before — does an instant-settlement rail change that?" is a seductive columnist angle, but the flop-history premise is not in the update; the proof note knows it, but the headline already spent the money.
gaps_in_A: "FedNow gets a merchant-facing on-ramp through Plaid's 12,000 bank connections" risks conflating Plaid's bank connectivity with actual FedNow-enabled reach; the proof section catches this, but the headline is still a little ahead of the evidence.

"a Plaid spokesperson willing to say plainly that this competes with card interchange" is less important than hard pricing disclosure or merchant validation; a company quote alone won't carry the incumbent-challenge angle.
The set mentions "large-ticket sellers" but never turns that into a clean vertical targeting lens; a founder still needs to know which merchant categories or trade desks to chase first.
gaps_in_B: "Bank-to-bank payments have flopped at checkout before" imports a historical premise absent from the update. Asking for sourcing later does not launder an unsupported headline.

"routing merchant payments through instant, FedNow-based settlement" overstates the facts; the update says instant bank verification and FedNow rails, not that settlement is wholly instant or FedNow-based.
"furniture, travel, auto, B2B invoicing" are plausible high-ticket examples, but they are not supplied facts. Mark them as hypotheses, not implied evidence.

"every angle here is currently unprovable without one" is too absolute. A named merchant would help, but the infrastructure and interchange-economics stories could still run with pricing, rail mechanics, and analyst or acquirer sourcing.
